title: Anatomy: Major Muscles
description: For anatomy students reviewing 50 major muscles through separate origin, insertion, and action prompts. Attachments are concise summaries of standard anatomy; verify with current guidelines for clinical use.

sources.name: Original wording from standard gross anatomy knowledge
OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, chapter 11, factual cross-check

cards.front: What is the origin of Masseter?
cards.back: Zygomatic arch and adjacent zygomatic bone.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Masseter?
cards.back: Lateral mandibular ramus and angle.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Masseter?
cards.back: Elevates the mandible to close the jaw; superficial fibers also assist protrusion.

cards.front: What is the origin of Temporalis?
cards.back: Temporal fossa and deep temporal fascia.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Temporalis?
cards.back: Coronoid process and anterior border of the mandibular ramus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Temporalis?
cards.back: Elevates the mandible; posterior fibers retract it.

cards.front: What is the origin of Sternocleidomastoid?
cards.back: Manubrium of the sternum and medial clavicle.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Sternocleidomastoid?
cards.back: Mastoid process and lateral part of the superior nuchal line.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Sternocleidomastoid?
cards.back: Unilaterally bends the neck to the same side and rotates the face to the opposite side; bilateral action flexes the cervical region and can extend the head.

cards.front: What is the origin of Trapezius?
cards.back: Occipital bone, ligamentum nuchae, and spinous processes from C7 through T12.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Trapezius?
cards.back: Lateral clavicle, acromion, and scapular spine.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Trapezius?
cards.back: Elevates, retracts, depresses, and upwardly rotates the scapula through different fiber groups.

cards.front: What is the origin of Levator scapulae?
cards.back: Transverse processes of C1-C4.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Levator scapulae?
cards.back: Medial scapular border superior to the scapular spine.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Levator scapulae?
cards.back: Elevates and downwardly rotates the scapula.

cards.front: What is the origin of Rhomboid minor?
cards.back: Lower ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7-T1.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Rhomboid minor?
cards.back: Medial scapular border at the root of the scapular spine.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Rhomboid minor?
cards.back: Retracts and downwardly rotates the scapula; helps hold it against the thoracic wall.

cards.front: What is the origin of Rhomboid major?
cards.back: Spinous processes of T2-T5.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Rhomboid major?
cards.back: Medial scapular border below the spine, extending toward the inferior angle.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Rhomboid major?
cards.back: Retracts and downwardly rotates the scapula; stabilizes it against the thoracic wall.

cards.front: What is the origin of Serratus anterior?
cards.back: External surfaces of the upper eight or nine ribs.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Serratus anterior?
cards.back: Anterior surface of the medial scapular border.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Serratus anterior?
cards.back: Protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula and holds it against the thoracic wall.

cards.front: What is the origin of Pectoralis minor?
cards.back: Anterior surfaces of ribs 3-5 near their costal cartilages.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Pectoralis minor?
cards.back: Coracoid process of the scapula.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Pectoralis minor?
cards.back: Draws the scapula anteriorly and inferiorly; can assist inspiration when the scapula is fixed.

cards.front: What is the origin of Pectoralis major?
cards.back: Medial clavicle, sternum, upper costal cartilages, and external oblique aponeurosis.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Pectoralis major?
cards.back: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Pectoralis major?
cards.back: Adducts and medially rotates the arm; clavicular fibers flex it, and sternocostal fibers extend it from a flexed position.

cards.front: What is the origin of Latissimus dorsi?
cards.back: Lower thoracic spinous processes, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lower ribs; a scapular slip may occur.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Latissimus dorsi?
cards.back: Floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Latissimus dorsi?
cards.back: Extends, adducts, and medially rotates the arm at the shoulder.

cards.front: What is the origin of Deltoid?
cards.back: Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, and scapular spine.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Deltoid?
cards.back: Deltoid tuberosity of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Deltoid?
cards.back: Middle fibers abduct the arm; anterior fibers flex and medially rotate it; posterior fibers extend and laterally rotate it.

cards.front: What is the origin of Supraspinatus?
cards.back: Supraspinous fossa of the scapula.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Supraspinatus?
cards.back: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Supraspinatus?
cards.back: Initiates and assists arm abduction and stabilizes the humeral head in the glenoid cavity.

cards.front: What is the origin of Infraspinatus?
cards.back: Infraspinous fossa of the scapula.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Infraspinatus?
cards.back: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Infraspinatus?
cards.back: Laterally rotates the arm and stabilizes the shoulder joint.

cards.front: What is the origin of Teres minor?
cards.back: Lateral border of the scapula, chiefly its upper part.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Teres minor?
cards.back: Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Teres minor?
cards.back: Laterally rotates the arm, assists adduction, and stabilizes the shoulder joint.

cards.front: What is the origin of Subscapularis?
cards.back: Subscapular fossa on the anterior scapula.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Subscapularis?
cards.back: Lesser tubercle of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Subscapularis?
cards.back: Medially rotates the arm, assists adduction, and stabilizes the shoulder joint.

cards.front: What is the origin of Teres major?
cards.back: Posterior surface of the inferior angle and adjacent lateral border of the scapula.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Teres major?
cards.back: Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Teres major?
cards.back: Adducts, extends, and medially rotates the arm.

cards.front: What is the origin of Coracobrachialis?
cards.back: Coracoid process of the scapula.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Coracobrachialis?
cards.back: Middle part of the medial humeral shaft.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Coracobrachialis?
cards.back: Flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder.

cards.front: What is the origin of Biceps brachii?
cards.back: Long head: supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula; short head: coracoid process.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Biceps brachii?
cards.back: Radial tuberosity and forearm fascia through the bicipital aponeurosis.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Biceps brachii?
cards.back: Supinates the forearm and flexes the elbow; assists shoulder flexion.

cards.front: What is the origin of Brachialis?
cards.back: Distal half of the anterior humerus.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Brachialis?
cards.back: Coronoid process and tuberosity of the ulna.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Brachialis?
cards.back: Flexes the elbow regardless of forearm pronation or supination.

cards.front: What is the origin of Brachioradialis?
cards.back: Proximal part of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Brachioradialis?
cards.back: Lateral distal radius just proximal to the styloid process.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Brachioradialis?
cards.back: Flexes the elbow most effectively with the forearm in a neutral position.

cards.front: What is the origin of Triceps brachii?
cards.back: Long head: infraglenoid tubercle; lateral head: posterior humerus above the radial groove; medial head: posterior humerus below the groove.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Triceps brachii?
cards.back: Olecranon of the ulna.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Triceps brachii?
cards.back: Extends the elbow; the long head also extends and adducts the arm at the shoulder.

cards.front: What is the origin of Anconeus?
cards.back: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Anconeus?
cards.back: Lateral olecranon and proximal posterior ulna.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Anconeus?
cards.back: Assists elbow extension and stabilizes the elbow joint.

cards.front: What is the origin of Pronator teres?
cards.back: Medial epicondyle of the humerus and coronoid process of the ulna.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Pronator teres?
cards.back: Middle of the lateral surface of the radius.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Pronator teres?
cards.back: Pronates the forearm and weakly assists elbow flexion.

cards.front: What is the origin of Pronator quadratus?
cards.back: Distal anterior ulna.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Pronator quadratus?
cards.back: Distal anterior radius.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Pronator quadratus?
cards.back: Pronates the forearm and helps bind the distal radius and ulna together.

cards.front: What is the origin of Supinator?
cards.back: Lateral epicondyle, radial collateral and annular ligaments, and supinator crest of the ulna.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Supinator?
cards.back: Proximal third of the radius on its lateral, anterior, and posterior surfaces.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Supinator?
cards.back: Supinates the forearm.

cards.front: What is the origin of Flexor carpi radialis?
cards.back: Medial epicondyle of the humerus through the common flexor tendon.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Flexor carpi radialis?
cards.back: Base of the second metacarpal, often with a slip to the third.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Flexor carpi radialis?
cards.back: Flexes and abducts the hand at the wrist; abduction here is radial deviation.

cards.front: What is the origin of Flexor carpi ulnaris?
cards.back: Medial epicondyle, olecranon, and posterior border of the ulna.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Flexor carpi ulnaris?
cards.back: Pisiform, with ligamentous continuations to the hook of hamate and base of the fifth metacarpal.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Flexor carpi ulnaris?
cards.back: Flexes and adducts the hand at the wrist; adduction here is ulnar deviation.

cards.front: What is the origin of Palmaris longus?
cards.back: Medial epicondyle of the humerus through the common flexor tendon.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Palmaris longus?
cards.back: Flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Palmaris longus?
cards.back: Tenses the palmar aponeurosis and weakly flexes the wrist; the muscle is absent in some people.

cards.front: What is the origin of Extensor carpi radialis longus?
cards.back: Distal part of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Extensor carpi radialis longus?
cards.back: Dorsal base of the second metacarpal.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Extensor carpi radialis longus?
cards.back: Extends and abducts the hand at the wrist.

cards.front: What is the origin of Extensor carpi radialis brevis?
cards.back: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus through the common extensor tendon.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Extensor carpi radialis brevis?
cards.back: Dorsal base of the third metacarpal.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Extensor carpi radialis brevis?
cards.back: Extends and abducts the hand at the wrist.

cards.front: What is the origin of Extensor carpi ulnaris?
cards.back: Lateral epicondyle and posterior border of the ulna.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Extensor carpi ulnaris?
cards.back: Dorsal base of the fifth metacarpal.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Extensor carpi ulnaris?
cards.back: Extends and adducts the hand at the wrist.

cards.front: What is the origin of Rectus abdominis?
cards.back: Pubic crest and pubic symphysis.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Rectus abdominis?
cards.back: Xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5-7.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Rectus abdominis?
cards.back: Flexes the trunk, compresses abdominal contents, and assists posterior pelvic tilt.

cards.front: What is the origin of External oblique?
cards.back: External surfaces of ribs 5-12.

cards.front: What is the insertion of External oblique?
cards.back: Linea alba, pubic tubercle, and anterior iliac crest through muscle and aponeurosis.

cards.front: What is the principal action of External oblique?
cards.back: Compresses the abdomen; bilaterally flexes the trunk and unilaterally rotates it to the opposite side.

cards.front: What is the origin of Internal oblique?
cards.back: Thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lateral part of the inguinal ligament.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Internal oblique?
cards.back: Lower ribs, linea alba, and pubis through the conjoint tendon.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Internal oblique?
cards.back: Compresses the abdomen; bilaterally flexes the trunk and unilaterally rotates it to the same side.

cards.front: What is the origin of Transversus abdominis?
cards.back: Internal surfaces of lower costal cartilages, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lateral inguinal ligament.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Transversus abdominis?
cards.back: Linea alba and pubis through its aponeurosis and conjoint tendon.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Transversus abdominis?
cards.back: Compresses and supports abdominal contents and contributes to trunk stability.

cards.front: What is the origin of Gluteus maximus?
cards.back: Posterior ilium, dorsal sacrum and coccyx, and sacrotuberous ligament.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Gluteus maximus?
cards.back: Iliotibial tract and gluteal tuberosity of the femur.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Gluteus maximus?
cards.back: Extends and laterally rotates the thigh, especially during rising or climbing.

cards.front: What is the origin of Gluteus medius?
cards.back: External ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Gluteus medius?
cards.back: Lateral surface of the greater trochanter.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Gluteus medius?
cards.back: Abducts the thigh and stabilizes the pelvis during single-leg stance; anterior fibers assist medial rotation.

cards.front: What is the origin of Gluteus minimus?
cards.back: External ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Gluteus minimus?
cards.back: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Gluteus minimus?
cards.back: Abducts and medially rotates the thigh and stabilizes the pelvis during walking.

cards.front: What is the origin of Tensor fasciae latae?
cards.back: Anterior superior iliac spine and adjacent anterior iliac crest.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Tensor fasciae latae?
cards.back: Iliotibial tract, which continues to the lateral tibial condyle.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Tensor fasciae latae?
cards.back: Flexes, abducts, and medially rotates the thigh; tensions the iliotibial tract to help stabilize the knee.

cards.front: What is the origin of Sartorius?
cards.back: Anterior superior iliac spine.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Sartorius?
cards.back: Superior medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Sartorius?
cards.back: Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh; flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg.

cards.front: What is the origin of Rectus femoris?
cards.back: Anterior inferior iliac spine and ilium just superior to the acetabulum.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Rectus femoris?
cards.back: Patella through the quadriceps tendon, then tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Rectus femoris?
cards.back: Extends the knee and flexes the hip.

cards.front: What is the origin of Vastus lateralis?
cards.back: Greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Vastus lateralis?
cards.back: Patella through the quadriceps tendon, then tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Vastus lateralis?
cards.back: Extends the knee and contributes to patellar stability.

cards.front: What is the origin of Vastus medialis?
cards.back: Intertrochanteric line and medial lip of the linea aspera.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Vastus medialis?
cards.back: Patella through the quadriceps tendon, then tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Vastus medialis?
cards.back: Extends the knee; distal fibers help resist lateral displacement of the patella.

cards.front: What is the origin of Vastus intermedius?
cards.back: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Vastus intermedius?
cards.back: Patella through the quadriceps tendon, then tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Vastus intermedius?
cards.back: Extends the knee.

cards.front: What is the origin of Biceps femoris?
cards.back: Long head: ischial tuberosity; short head: linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Biceps femoris?
cards.back: Primarily the head of the fibula.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Biceps femoris?
cards.back: Flexes the knee and laterally rotates the flexed leg; the long head also extends the hip.

cards.front: What is the origin of Semitendinosus?
cards.back: Ischial tuberosity.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Semitendinosus?
cards.back: Superior medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Semitendinosus?
cards.back: Extends the hip, flexes the knee, and medially rotates the flexed leg.

cards.front: What is the origin of Semimembranosus?
cards.back: Ischial tuberosity.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Semimembranosus?
cards.back: Posterior part of the medial tibial condyle, with expansions including the oblique popliteal ligament.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Semimembranosus?
cards.back: Extends the hip, flexes the knee, and medially rotates the flexed leg.

cards.front: What is the origin of Gastrocnemius?
cards.back: Femur near the medial and lateral condyles.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Gastrocnemius?
cards.back: Posterior calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Gastrocnemius?
cards.back: Plantarflexes the ankle and flexes the knee.

cards.front: What is the origin of Soleus?
cards.back: Posterior proximal fibula, soleal line and medial border of the tibia, and a tendinous arch between the bones.

cards.front: What is the insertion of Soleus?
cards.back: Posterior calcaneus through the calcaneal tendon.

cards.front: What is the principal action of Soleus?
cards.back: Plantarflexes the ankle and supports posture while standing; it does not cross the knee.
